chunks: Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abi Ja'far عليه السلام: How is it that ghusl becomes obligatory upon a woman if she sees in sleep that a man has intercourse with her in her farj, yet ghusl is not made obligatory upon her if he has intercourse with her short of the farj while awake and she emits fluid?

He عليه السلام said: Because she saw in her dream that a man had intercourse with her in her farj, so ghusl became obligatory upon her. As for the other case, he only had intercourse with her short of the farj, so ghusl did not become obligatory upon her because he did not insert it. But if he had inserted it while awake, ghusl would have become obligatory upon her whether she emitted fluid or did not emit.

key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ritual bath that becomes obligatory after certain states of janabah
key_terms.دُونَ الْفَرْجِ: short of the farj; meaning contact or intercourse without vaginal penetration
key_terms.فَأَمْنَتْ: she emitted fluid; referring to female emission
key_terms.فِي النَّوْمِ: in sleep; indicating the case of a dream state
key_terms.فِي الْيَقَظَةِ: in wakefulness; distinguishing the waking state from sleep
key_terms.فِي فَرْجِهَا: in her farj; referring to vaginal intercourse as the legal cause discussed
key_terms.لَمْ يُدْخِلْهُ: he did not insert it; identifying the absence of penetration
key_terms.وَجَبَ عَلَيْهَا: it became obligatory upon her; indicating legal obligation

ai.seo_question: When does ghusl become obligatory for a woman in cases of dream intercourse or contact without penetration?
ai.summary: This hadith explains a legal ruling concerning ghusl for a woman in cases of dream intercourse and physical contact short of vaginal penetration. The ruling turns on the occurrence of intercourse in the farj, not merely on emission, and clarifies that penetration in wakefulness obligates ghusl whether emission occurs or not.
